## Hard-to-vary check: Church-Turing thesis entry

**1. The question, frozen.** The entry’s title and opening make central: *What is the Church-Turing thesis, and how does it turn the informal notion of an effective method into a precise claim?* Range: logic, mathematics, computer science; methods a human can carry out with paper and pencil, without insight. Asked: partly a definition, partly an argument for why the formal replacement is accepted. I freeze that. The history and *Entscheidungsproblem* material are secondary.

**2. The explanation in parts.**

P1. Four criteria for an “effective” method.  
P2. The informal notion lacks rigor; “no insight” is unexplicated.  
P3. Church and Turing offer different formal predicates; these pick out the same class *S*.  
P4. The Church-Turing thesis: *S* contains every function obtainable by an effective method, and vice versa.  
P5. Turing machines and computable numbers give the formal model.  
P6. Turing’s argument I: features 1–9 of human computation, then a *B-L*-type machine, then ordinary Turing machine simulation.  
P7. States of mind replaced by *m*-configurations or notes of instructions.  
P8. Turing’s argument II: equivalence with provability in Hilbert’s calculus.  
P9. Inductive and equivalence evidence, plus skepticism.  
P10. The *Entscheidungsproblem* and historical backstory.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 Four criteria | **Fixed** | The owner sets these as the term of art. Removing “no insight” would change the question, not test the thesis. |
| P2 Informal, lacks rigor | **Held** | Remove it and the need for a formal replacement disappears. |
| P3 Church/Turing predicates equivalent | **Two routes** | Either Church’s recursion/λ-definability or Turing’s machines does the job of formalizing effectiveness. Both pick out the same class. |
| P4 Church-Turing thesis | **Held if** | It holds only if Turing’s analysis of human computation is right. Skeptics doubt the finite-state and no-insight assumptions. |
| P5 Turing machine model | **Held** | It is a formal definition. Change the machine and the computable set changes in a checkable way. |
| P6 Argument I, features 1–9 | **Held if** | Features 2–5 and 8 do visible work. Feature 1, two-dimensional paper to one-dimensional tape, is questioned. Features 6–7 and 9, finite states of mind, carry the thesis; if they fail, the thesis breaks. |
| P7 States of mind as notes | **Held if** | It is a patch for the mind worry. It holds only if the notes remain finite and demand no insight. |
| P8 Argument II | **Held if** | It proves an equivalence with a logic. It supports the thesis only if the new definition already has intuitive appeal. |
| P9 Inductive/equivalence evidence | **Loose** | Past computable functions could be swapped for other past functions. Equivalence shows “if one is true, all are,” not that any is true. |
| P10 History/Entscheidungsproblem | **Idle** | For the frozen question, the definition and support stand without it. It would be held if the question were historical. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**

**Flip.** Had the thesis been false, what would we see? A human effective method that no Turing machine can simulate. The entry says this would be a surprise and would break the thesis. It does not explain the opposite just as smoothly. Good.

**Direction.** The argument runs forward: from features of human computation to a machine that copies them. It is not merely working backward from “Turing machines compute these functions.”

**Answer hidden?** The conclusion is not simply put into the starting points under another name. The entry defines “effective” and then states the thesis as a thesis. The weak point is that “no insight” is a negative catch-all. The states-of-mind discussion acts as a gauge: it tries to show what would count as a method needing insight or infinitely many states.

**Jobs and where they came from.** Most jobs are given by the subject: define effectiveness, state the thesis, prove equivalence, defend it. The skeptic jobs are added by critics. The historical jobs are added by the entry. The central support job is given, not invented by the tester.

**Pairs that pull.** Precision pulls against intuitive appeal. Turing’s argument I is more convincing than Church’s because it starts from human computation, but that also makes it depend on an intuitive list of features. Tighten “no insight” too much and you may exclude real human computation; loosen it and the thesis becomes trivial. The line is drawn at finite states of mind. What would show the line wrong: a human computation with infinitely many distinguishable states or with non-local observation.

**Catch-all and gauge.** “No insight, intuition, or ingenuity” is a catch-all. Its gauge is the finite-state/notes discussion and Gödel’s worry that the mind develops. Without that gauge, the phrase would swallow any failure.

**Change list.** The thesis covers any effective method by a human with paper and pencil, no insight. It leaves out non-effective methods and non-human physical computation. It mostly says this out loud: computation in 1936 meant human computation.

**Rivals.** Church’s thesis, Post’s systems, Gandy’s axioms, and Dershowitz-Gurevich’s postulates are rivals at the level of formulation. On the class of functions they are the same. Turing’s adds the machine picture. No listed change separates them on the class; a finer question would ask about the machine meaning.

**Where the parts came from.** The definitions are **fixed**. Equivalence proofs are **borrowed** from Church, Kleene, and Turing. Argument I is **built**, though on an intuitive base. Inductive evidence is **fitted** to past cases. History is **borrowed**.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Turn features 1–9 into explicit axioms and try to derive the thesis from them. Then look for one concrete case where an effective method needs infinite states or non-local observation. Also add a job: every new model of computation—parallel, interactive, quantum—must be simulable by a Turing machine. If one is not, the thesis is caught out.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. The thesis may be true even though its support is partly inductive and partly intuitive. Loose parts may be right. The entry is expository, so much of its strength is borrowed from proofs and history rather than built here.

**7. One next step.** Write the essential features 1–9 as premises and test each one against a possible counterexample—especially finite states of mind and two-dimensional paper—to see which premise would have to fall.
